Initial studies if Crohn’s is suspected should include CBC, metabolic profile, stool for lactoferrin, calprotectin and clostridium difficile, and ileocolonoscopy. Histopathological evaluation ultimately remains the gold diagnostic standard for Crohn's.C
Crohn’s disease is classified into mild-moderate, moderate-severe, or severe-fulminant depending on clinical presentation, treatment response, and complications (see ). C

Treatment is based on disease severity and can involve corticosteroids for induction of remission, and anti-TNF drugs, vedolizumab, upadacitinib, and IL-12 and 23 blockers for both induction and maintenance of remission. A

Complications are common and include fistulae, abscesses, and obstructions, which may require surgical intervention and/or IV antibiotics. B Systemic complications include osteoporosis, skin rashes, eye irritation, and cancers. C

background.definition: Crohn’s disease is a chronic inflammatory disease that usually affects the ileum and colon but can occur in any part of the intestinal tract. It causes transmural, discontinuous lesions in the bowel that are often complicated by obstruction, abscess, and fistulae. It has the potential for systemic complications often manifesting in the joints, skin, and eyes. Phenotypic classification is based on the Montreal () or Paris classification.

list.listitem: Incidence is 13/100,000 persons per year in the United States
Age of onset is typically in a bimodal distribution between 15 to 35 years and 55 to 70 years.
Prevalence is approximately 165/100,000 persons in the United States.
The cost of medical and surgical therapy per person was estimated at up to $27,000 annually in the United States in 2020, as compared to $7,000 for those not diagnosed with Crohn's disease.
Genetic and environmental risk factors are equally important in the appearance and progression.
Studies demonstrate a 23% prevalence in first-degree relatives of Crohn’s disease (CD) patients and 65% concordance in monozygotic twins.

Among families with multiple affected members, there tends to be a fairly high degree of clinical similarity for disease location, behavior, age at the time of diagnosis and the presence of extra-intestinal manifestations of the disease

There is an association between diet and intestinal permeability in Crohn’s disease, but these have not been well established or translated into practical considerations for management. Exclusive enteral nutrition with a liquid diet is currently used as a first-line diet therapy in children with Crohn'. It is shown to improve clinical, biomarker, endoscopic, and radiologic findings in adults as well, yet it remains a difficult treatment for adults who are more reluctant to have a liquid only diet via NG tube.

A narrative review analyzes the possible role of the Mediterranean diet on Crohn's disease. It demonstrates the benefits of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and nuts as anti-inflammatory to the gut. The diet is rich in fiber,however, meaning it may be difficult for patients with no active disease

A meta analysis of 16 epidemiological studies found no association between alcohol or coffee intake with development of Crohn’s disease. High soft drink consumption was associated with a higher CD risk (RR 1.42, 95% CI 1.01-1.98), while high tea consumption was associated with decreased risk (RR 0.70, 95% CI, 0.53-0.93).
Other lifestyle factors like smoking, and medical histories including appendectomy and tonsillectomy have been associated with increased risk. 139
Canned and processed foods, alcohol, and other sweetened beverages should be avoided as they are not part of the Groningen anti-inflammatory diet that impacts the onset and course of Crohn's disease.
There is no association between the development of inflammatory bowel disease and birthing via cesarean section.

A systematic review of eight case-control and three cohort studies found an association between Crohn's disease and previous antibiotic use, especially metronidazole and fluoroquinolones. Causality has not been demonstrated, and it is possible that antibiotics were given for early symptoms of CD in these patients. It has been proposed that this association is due to the hygiene hypothesis, which states that our increased development of inflammatory bowel disease is secondary to decreased infectious disease and increased antibiotic use earlier in life.
A 2024 systemic review and meta-analysis involving 28 studies demonstrated significant association with metronidazole and fluoroquinolones use and increased new onset IBD.
Increased visceral adiposity was found to be an independent risk factor for recurrence in post-endoscopic patients.
Smoking and oral contraceptive use increase the risk of recurrence.
Intercurrent infections (including respiratory and enteric infections) and NSAID use exacerbate disease.
There is no association between measles vaccination and the development of inflammatory bowel disease.
The pathophysiology of Crohn’s disease has not been definitively described, but is believed to result from immune dysregulation within the intestine that leads to a chronic inflammatory state.
Mesenteric or "creeping" fat around the circumference of the intestine is pathognomonic and may even play a role in the pathogenesis of Crohn's disease due to containing immune cells.
The resulting overproduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines leads to well-demarcated, discontinuous, transmural lesions with a tendency to form fistulae.
There is a clear genetic component, given 65% concordance in monozygotic twins.
Mitochondrial damage involving impaired oxidative phosphorylation is thought to contribute to IBD development as it contributes to breakdown of intestinal barrier.

Colorectal cancer is more common in patients with inflammatory bowel disease, and there is indirect evidence that surveillance may improve outcomes (primarily stage at diagnosis). However, this could represent lead-time bias. Screening in this group is not addressed by the USPSTF or ACS. C

A nested case-control study showed that combined oral contraceptives increase the likelihood of relapse in patients with Crohn’s disease (OR 1.60, 95% CI, 1.41-1.82); women should consider alternative forms of birth control. Use of oral birth control pills and parenteral contraceptive methods were not associated with an increased risk of Crohn's disease relapse compared to those who don't use any form of birth control (OR 1.09, 95% CI .84-1.4 and OR 1.15, 95% CI .99-1.47, respectively). B

Smoking increases the risk of recurrence, whether you are a current smoker or former smoker (OR 4.16, 95% CI, .6-8.27 and OR 1.16, 95% CI .52-8.09, respectively); patients who smoke should be encouraged to quit.B

A cost-effectiveness analysis found that chemoprophylaxis against pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia is not helpful specifically due to monetary concern. However, a case series study highlighted the need for prophylactic therapy in immunosuppressed patients for the concern of potentially fatal PJP.
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs may worsen disease activity and should be avoided if possible.B
Consider Crohn’s disease when patients present with chronic or nocturnal diarrhea, abdominal pain, anemia, fatigue, weight loss, fever, or symptoms indicating an intestinal blockage or fistula. C

Initial labs should include CBC, metabolic profile, and a stool sample for Clostridium difficile, lactoferrin, and calprotectin. Fecal calprotectin is useful when negative for ruling out Crohn's disease in adults and children.C
Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and confirmed with endoscopic (including histologic) findings. C
Crohn’s disease is classified into mild-moderate, moderate-severe, or severe-fulminant depending on clinical presentation, treatment response, and complications (see ). C

list.listitem: ACG guidelines (2025) recommend that Crohn's be considered when a patient presents with chronic (>6 weeks) or nocturnal diarrhea, abdominal pain (especially RLQ), weight loss, fever, fatigue, anemia, or symptoms indicating an intestinal blockage or fistula. Younger patients may initially present with growth failure as well.

The medical history should include symptom onset, duration, recent travel, food intolerance, sick contacts, medication use, smoking, and family history. Typical historical findings include abdominal pain, weight loss, diarrhea, fatigue, fever, or rectal bleeding. Of all the symptoms listed above, the most common presenting in Crohn's were tiredness/fatigue (80.6%) and abdominal pain (80.4%).

A study of 1981 adults with lower GI symptoms presenting to a gastroenterologist for evaluation, of whom 302 had CD or UC, found that individual signs and symptoms had low predictive value. Absence of bloody stools had a LR− of 0.7, while passage of stools more than 4 times a day had a LR+ of 2.3.

Measure weight and perform a rectal exam with occult blood testing. The physical exam may show pallor, cachexia, abdominal tenderness or mass, perianal fissures (10% of patients), fistulae, or abscess. Clubbing may be present.
Extraintestinal manifestations may be present even in the absence of the typical signs/symptoms and include inflammation of eyes, skin, or joints; or delay of growth or puberty in children.
See for severity classification.

Physical evaluation of lesions of the lips, mucosa, and gingivae can provide key information for early diagnosis of Crohn's disease. The most common types of lesions are ulcers, gingivitis, and angular cheilitis.
While Crohn's disease is a diagnosis based on both clinical and endoscopic features, histopathological evaluation remains a gold standard at this time.

American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) guidelines (2025) recommend fecal calprotectinn with a cutoff of > 50-100 mcg/gram to distinguish inflammatory from non-inflammatory bowel disease. At initial presentation tests for dehydration, malnutrition, and anemia are indicated. Stool testing should include fecal pathogens, C. difficile testing, and fecal calprotectin.
They recommend against genetic testing or use of inflammatory biomarkers such as ESR or CRP to make the diagnosis.

Several novel blood tests accurately distinguish Crohn’s disease (or other inflammatory bowel disease) from irritable bowel syndrome and other non-inflammatory bowel conditions. They include fecal lactoferrin (LR+ 45, LR− 0.1), fecal calprotectin (LR+ 10.6, LR− 0.1), and anti-Saccaromyces cerevisiae antibodies (ASCA). Fecal calprotectin has the strongest evidence for its use and is recommended by ACG guidelines (2025). Note that anti-neutrophil cytoplasm antibodies (ANCA) suggest ulcerative colitis, not Crohn's disease. Thus, the combination of positive ASCA and negative pANCA strongly suggests Crohn's disease. A systematic review of 8 studies of fecal calprotectin in children found that it had a very good sensitivity (95%-100%) and negative predictive value (3% with pretest probability of 50%).

A study in children in the primary care setting with clinically suspected inflammatory bowel disease found that fecal calprotectin was 100% sensitive and 91% specific. When the fecal calprotectin result was negative, it effectively ruled out inflammatory bowel disease. The LR+ was 11.1 and LR- was 0.0 (95% CI of 0.0 to 0.3). It is important to note that fecal calprotectin can be raised by many illnesses and medications. Fecal calprotectin should not be measured during acute and short-term diarrhea or bloody stool (<14 days) and should always be accompanied by a stool bacterial and viral screen.

As the availability of fecal calprotectin has increased, so has the false positive referral rate to gastroenterology. Repeating the fecal calprotectin if the initial result was only mildly elevated can help stratify the urgency of the referral to specialist care.

Clostridium difficile infection is part of the differential diagnosis of Crohn’s disease and can be comorbid with it; this may obscure the diagnosis initially. Stool examination for Clostridium difficile toxin is recommended.

Newer data also suggest the use of biomarkers identified via metabolomics and proteomics in the urine. Hippurate and formate were identified as potential biomarkers of disease activity and clinical relapse. With further testing, having strong urinary biomarkers could offer a cheaper, less invasive, promising alternative to endoscopies/colonoscopies as a means to identifyng Crohn's.

For suspected Crohn’s, ileocolonoscopy with multiple biopsies is recommended by ACG guidelines (2025) as the first-line procedure to establish the diagnosis. Apparently uninvolved areas should be biopsied to establish the extent of histologic disease.
ACG guidelines (2025) and British guidelines recommend upper endoscopy for patients with upper gastrointestinal symptoms.

Imaging using contrast magnetic resonance enterography or small bowel ultrasound to detect small bowel disease is also recommended by British and ACG guidelines, especially for younger patients, with CT as an alternative.

Capsule endoscopy is an alternative to endoscopy and imaging in patients with a high clinical suspicion of Crohn's disease (i.e. clinical picture and elevated fecal calprotectin) who have abstained from NSAIDs for at least one month. Bowel patency should be confirmed prior to the procedure to reduce the risk of capsule retention.
Small intestine contrast ultrasonography is sensitive and specific for the detection of small bowel lesions in patients with Crohn's (94% sensitive 95% CI 87-97%, 97% specific 95% CI 75%-95%).

When extramural complications are suspected (such as abscess or fistula), an imaging study such as ultrasound, CT, or MR colonography should be performed. In the United States, CT (or pelvic MRI to assess perianal fistula disease) are the most commonly selected imaging studies.

Issues around the use of the CT scan for patients with IBD still remain, however. One study demonstrated particularly high rates of CT utilization in Crohn's patients in the emergency room. Only 1/3 of scans demonstrated urgent findings, with a minority demonstrating uregent penetrating findings. Overall, clinicians tends to overscan patients with IBD-related concerns, and work should be done to identify patients in whom scanning is necessary to minimize radiation exposure risk.
Consider Crohn’s when patients present with chronic (>6 weeks) or nocturnal diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, fever, or symptoms indicating an intestinal blockage or fistula.

The general diagnostic approach is to rule out other causes of diarrhea before using endoscopy to identify characteristic lesions. When diarrhea is present, rule out enteric pathogens by testing a stool sample for lactoferrin and Clostridium difficile.
Initial laboratory investigations should include CBC, metabolic profiles and fecal calprotectin.
Assess for extraintestinal manifestations.
Refer patients for ileocolonoscopy and imaging to confirm the diagnosis, to obtain samples for histopathologic evaluation, and to assess disease location and severity.

Disease is classified into mild-moderate, moderate-severe, severe-fulminant, or remission depending on clinical presentation, treatment response, and complications (). Phenotypic classification uses the Montreal () or Paris classifications.
Treatment is based on the severity of disease, phase of disease (flare or remission) and response to earlier treatment modalities. C
Controlled ileal release budesonide is recommended for induction of remission of mild to moderate active disease.A

Systemic steroids have adverse side effects and should only be used to induce remission temporarily in moderate-severe disease. Methotrexate and thiopurines are immunomodulators utilized in maintenance therapy to lessen corticosteroid requirements.A

For maintenance of remission, a thiopurine (azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine) or methotrexate is recommended. Anti-TNF agents, vedolizumab, anti-interleukin 12 and/or 23 agents, and upadacitinib are other classes of medication used to induce and maintain remission in moderate to severe Crohn's disease. If an anti-TNF inhibitor was used to induce remission, it should be continued for maintenance of remission.B
For patients with severe/fulminant disease, hospitalization and IV corticosteroids are initial therapy.B

Fistulae should be treated with antibiotics and perirectal abscesses should be treated with surgical drainage prior to medical therapy. Obstruction treatment depends on the type of obstruction but surgical consultation is warranted. B
American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) guidelines (2025) recommend that advanced therapy not be contingent on failure of conventional therapies.
For patients with asymptomatic, mild Crohn's disease (CD) regular monitoring without medical therapy is an option.

ACG guidelines (2025) recommend controlled ileal release budesonide 9 mg once daily for induction of remission (but not maintenance of remission) in patients with CD of the terminal ilium and right colon. Oral mesalamine, metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, and antimycobacterial therapy are not recommended. For patients with mild disease and low risk of progression, treatment with sulfasalazine, anti-diarrheals or dietary manipulation are also an option.

Mesalamine 3.2 to 4 g daily and sulfasalazine (ileocolonic or colonic only) 3 to 6 g daily have traditionally been recommended. However, recent systematic reviews have found that they are little better than placebo and are less effective than budesonide, especially in patients with active flares. The ACG guidelines (2025) recommend against using mesalamine at all during periods of active inflammation.

Antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, and rifaximin have been shown to be no more effectiveness than placebo as therapy for luminal Crohn's disease and should not be used as primary therapy. They are useful as adjunctive therapy in patients with fistulas, though.

Anti-tubercular therapies are not effective, and the evidence base is insufficient for disease limited to the upper GI tract. If treatment is unsuccessful, advance to treatment for moderate to severe disease.

For patients with low risk of disease progression, treatment of symptoms with antidiarrheals, other nonspecific medications, and dietary manipulation, along with careful observation for inadequate symptom relief, worsening inflammation, or disease progression, is acceptable.

ACG guidelines (2025) recommend beginning with an oral corticosteroid for patients with moderate to severe active disease. Both oral prednisone 40 to 60 mg daily and oral budesonide 3 mg tid are effective compared with placebo, and are generally given for 1 to 2 weeks and then tapered by 5 mg per week over no more than 3 months. A Cochrane review of 9 studies with 779 patients found that budesonide is slightly less effective than prednisone, but has fewer side effects.

Despite their efficacy in reducing signs and symptoms of active Crohn's disease, nearly 1 in 5 people will prove to be steroid refractory while an additional 1/3 will become steroid dependent, unable to taper without subsequent symptom recurrence. For these reasons, oral corticosteroids should be used sparingly and for no longer than 3 months at a time.

The thiopurines azathioprine (at doses 1.5 to 2.5 mg/kg/day) and 6-mercaptopurine (at doses 0.75 to 1.5 mg/kg/day), as well as methotrexate (parenteral) can help maintain remission of moderately to severely active CD that has been induced by steroids, but are not recommended by 2025 ACG guidelines for induction of remission. They are effective for steroid-sparing. Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) testing is recommended prior to use of azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine. Methotrexate 25 mg IM or SC once weekly is also effective for maintenance of remission and are recommended by ACG guidelines (2025). Decrease dose to 15 mg/week at 4 months if in steroid-free remission.

For patients who do not respond to steroids or immunosuppressants, ACG guidelines (2025) recommend treatment with an anti-tumor necrosis factor (TNF) monoclonal antibody such as IV infliximab, SC adalimumab or SC certolizumab pegol for induction and maintenance of remission in moderate to severe CD.

Infliximab can be given with a thiopurine like azathioprine, and studies show this combination therapy is more effective than treatment with immunomodulators or infliximab alone. The anti-TNF drugs are also appropriate in patients who cannot take corticosteroids. An RCT randomized 508 patients to infliximab monotherapy, azathioprine monotherapy, or both. At 26 weeks, rates of steroid-free remission were 57% for combination therapy, 44% for infliximab alone, and 30% for azathioprine alone. Combination therapy of adalimumab or certolizumab pegol with an immunomodulator has not been well studied, but it is likely to be superior in efficacy than an anti-TNF drug alone given the immunogenicity of all biologics as well as the ability of immunomodulators to reduce the rate of anti-drug antibody formation.
Before starting an anti-TNF drug, patients should be tested for hepatitis B and tuberculosis.

ACG guidelines recommend SC infliximab for maintenance of remission for patients responding to induction with IV infliximab. Biosimilar versions of infliximab and adalimumab are acceptable for treatment.

An RCT of 244 adults with active Crohn's disease (CDAI 150 to 450 and Crohn's Disease Endoscopic Index of Severity >6) compared a strategy of escalation to adalimumab based on biomarkers plus clinical judgement versus clinical judgment alone. At one year, outcomes were better in the former group. A similar but smaller trial using infliximab, however, did not find an advantage to adding biomarkers to the decision-making process.A systematic review of adalimumab safety in 577 children being treated for a variety of conditions found that the rate of serious infections was 6.6 per 100 patient-years for those being treated for Crohn's.

The JAK inhibitor padacitinib is recommended for induction and maintenance of remission in patients with moderate to severe CD by the 2025 ACG guidelines. In the US use is limited to patients who have first tried an anti-TNF drug.

A clinical trial randomized 526 patients with moderate to severe Crohn's disease to the Janus kinase inhibitor upadacitinib 45 mg daily or placebo for a 12 week induction phase, followed by 15 mg, 30 mg or placebo during a one year maintenance phase. Clinical remission was significantly more likely with the active drug in both phases (NNT = 5).

In a 2024 meta-analysis, upadacitinib demonstrated significant efficacy in clinical remission and response as well as a favorable safety profile that makes it an effective alternative for patient's who are resistant and intolerant to first line therapy (immunosuppressants and tumor necrosis factor (TNF) antagonists).

Vedolizumab (a leukocyte trafficking inhibitor) is another medication that has been trialed for its effects in moderate to severe Crohn's disease and is recommended by 2025 ACG guidelines. It is the first gut selective biologic that works by binding integrin proteins within the digestive tract. A 2023 Cochrane review analyzed 4 induction and 3 maintenance trials with results showing that vedolizumab is superior to placebo in both the induction and maintenance phases in moderate to severe disease.With its favorable safety profile and no evidence of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, reactivation of TB or hepatitis B, vedolizumab can be given following treatment failure, combination therapy, or as a first-line monotherapy. While IV vedolizumab is required for induction, SC vedolizumab is an option for maintenance of remission.

Vedolizumab is another monoclonal antibody to integrin that has a favorable safety profile when used in combination therapy with immunosuppressives or as a maintenance drug after remission with corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors. No cases of PML, reactivation of tuberculosis or hepatitis B were identified during one year of follow-up. In another RCT, patients with moderately severe active CD who had failed therapy with a TNF antagonist were randomized to vedolizumab or placebo. There was no difference in outcomes at 6 weeks, but a greater likelihood of remission was seen at 10 weeks (27% vs 12%, p = 0.001, NNT = 7). More recently, a 2023 Cochrane review demonstrated that vedolizumab was superior to placebo for the induction of clinical remission (RR 1.61, 95% CI 1.2-2.17, NNT 13) and superior to placebo for inducing clinical response (RR 1.43, 95% CI 1.19-1.71, NNT 8)

ACG guidelines (2025) recommend ustekinumab, a targeted therapy for interleukins-12 and 23, an an option for induction and maintenance of remission in patients with moderate to severe CD. The guidelines also recommend risankizumab, mirikizumab and guselkizumab that target IL 23 for induction and maintenance of remission in patients with moderate to severe CD.

A meta-analysis of 18 trials concluded that targeting IL-23 for therapy was associated with a decrease risk of serious adverse events in induction of remission (RR= .55, 95% CI .44-.73) and maintenance of remission (RR=.72, 95% CI .53-.98) compared to placebo (high certainty evidence).

A study identified patients with moderate to severe Crohn's who did not tolerate anti TNF therapy. They were randomized to risankizuma of ustekinumab. Risankizumab had better clinical remission at week 24 (58.6% vs. 39.5%; 95% CI for risk difference 6.6 to 30.3) and was superior to ustekinumab for endoscopic remission at week 48 (31.8% vs. 16.2%, p < 0.001).

Ustekinumab is a monoclonal antibody against the p40 subunit of interleukin 12 and 23. Based on 3 RCTs with 334 patients who have moderate to severe Crohn's, it improved endoscopic healing compared with placebo. In an RCT with 251 patients with moderate to severe Crohn’s, histologic improvement was also seen compared with placebo. It is an option for patients not responding to other therapies including corticosteroids and anti-TNF inhibitors, and it has a favorable safety profile in the elderly population.

Mirikizumab is a humanized IgG4 anti-human IL-23 monoclonal antibody that was just approved in March 2023 in Japan for use in induction therapy in ulcerative colitis. It has been tested in patients with severe Crohn's disease, yet there is currently limited data in this population on its effectiveness and side effect profile.

The GRAVITI trial randomized 347 participants to guselkumab 400 mg every 4 weeks, stepping down to 100 mg every 8 weeks or 200 mg every 4 weeks or placebo. Significantly more patients experienced clinical remission compared to placebo (56.1% vs 21.4%, p < .001, NNT = 3).

An updated network meta-analysis identified 31 randomized trials comparing biologic therapies for moderate to severe CD. They concluded that infliximab with azathioprine or adalimumab were most likely to be the best first-line therapy, and adalimumab (after failed infliximab) or risankizumab are the best second line therapies.

In a 2024 meta-analysis, biologics were compared as treatments in patients with moderately to severely active Crohn's disease. Infliximab was found to be superior to all other agents. Risankizumab and adalimumab demonstrated the highest probability of early induction of remission.

The GALAXI-2 and 3 studies randomized 1048 patients with moderate to severe active Crohn's disease to 1) 200 mg IV guselkumab 200 mg every 4 weeks, 2) 200 mg guselkumab at weeks 0,4, 8 and then 100 mg every 4 weeks, 3) 6 mg/kg IV usetekinumab at week 0 then 90 mg subcutaneous ustekinumab every 8 weeks, or 4) IV placebo. Both guselkumab regimens were superior to placebo for clinical response at 12 weeks and remission at 48 weeks (49% to 55% versus 12%, p < 0.001, NNT = 2). The combination of clinical and endoscopic response was somewhat more likely with guselkumab than ustekinumab (42% to 47% versus 34%, p = 0.049 and 0.001 for difference).

Natalizumab is an option for patients that have not responded to or do not tolerate the above drugs, although can rarely cause progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) and is therefore not considered first-line therapy. Patients prescribed natalizumab should be tested for anti-John Cunningham virus antibody and only be given the medication if JC negative. They should be re-tested for anti-JC virus antibody.every 6 months while taking the medication.
In a RCT of 701 patients with active Crohn’s disease treated with mongerson, an antisense oligodeoxynucleotide to Smad7, did not show efficacy versus placebo in clinical trials.
A study concluded that there was no benefit to continuing 5-aminosaliclates in patients now being treated with biologic agents.

Hospitalize patients with severe or fulminant disease, or patients presenting with fever or other evidence of serious infection, inability to take oral fluids or medication, or evidence of peritonitis or obstruction. CT is recommended to exclude peritonitis or abscess, as well as consultation with a gastroenterologist. If serious infection is excluded, these patients should receive parenteral steroids (equivalent dose between 40 mg to 60 mg prednisone per day based on clinical picture).

ACG guidelines (2025) recommend IV infliximab for patients with severely active CD who are inpatients. NICE guidelines recommend that it be used for 12 months or until treatment failure, whichever is shorter. The NICE guidelines also recommend adalimumab as an alternative for patients with severe active Crohn's disease. Natalizumab 300 mg is an agent that is effective for induction and maintenance of remission in patients who have failed to respond to conventional treatments. However, its use is restricted to concerns about causing progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) and it should be.
ACG guidelines (2025) recommend infliximab for perianal, enterocutaneous, and rectovaginal fistulas. Adalimumab or certolizumab pegol are alternatives.

Azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine may be effective for fistulas, and tacrolimus is an option short-term. Antibiotics appear to be beneficial for simple perianal fistulas. Antibiotics plus infliximab were more effective than infliximab alone.
Abscesses should be drained prior to medical therapy with infliximab and/or antibiotics.
Placement of setons in combination with infliximab therapy increases the efficacy of infliximab and should be considered in treating perianal fistulas.

Once symptoms are in remission, patients should be treated with maintenance therapy. ACG guidelines (2025) recommend a thiopurine (azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine) or methotrexate for maintenance as steroid-sparing agents .

If an anti-TNF inhibitor such as infliximab, adalimumab or certolizumab pegol is used to induce remission, ACG guidelines recommend that one be continued to maintain remission. Use in combination with a thiopurine is recommended over anti-TNF monotherapy. If ustekinumab or vedolizumab were used to induce remission, the same drug should be used to maintain remission.

Interleukin 10, thalidomide and its analogues, and sargramostim are not effective for induction or maintenance of remission in Crohn’s, based on systematic reviews. A RCT with 280 patients found no significant benefit of tofacitinib for induction and maintenance of Crohn's disease.
Because Crohn’s disease occurs in discontinuous lesions throughout the GI tract, surgical cure is not possible.
For abscesses associated with fistulas, surgical drainage should be considered prior to instituting antibiotic therapy and/or infliximab.

Surgical consultation should be obtained if there is evidence (usually by CT, MR, or ultrasound) of abscess, fistula, abdominal mass, malignancy, or obstruction, if symptoms are refractory to medical therapy, or there is perianal disease.
Laparoscopic resection is an option for localized ileocecal disease following failure or relapse of medical therapy.

There is a low risk of occult cancer with colonic strictures so default surgical resection is not warranted, however, the need for resection for possible cancer should still be considered with new strictures, ones that cannot be traversed, or if other alarm features are present. Surgical resection may be necessary if strictures are also refractory to medical treatment.

Patients that had more mesentery removed during ileocolonic resection as compared to just ileocolonic resection had a decreased recurrence rate of disease at 2.9% compared to 40%. Visceral adiposity was found to be an independent risk factor for recurrence in post-endoscopic patients.
A systematic review identified 7 studies of 1125 patients comparing stapled with handsewn methods for ileocolic anastomosis. Staples resulted in fewer leaks.

A systematic review of population-based observational studies found that the 5-year risk of requiring a second surgery was 29% (95% CI, 23%-37%). The 10-year risk was 35% (95% CI, 32%-39%). Newer studies had a lower likelihood of requiring a second surgery, probably due to improved medical therapy options.

While surgical therapy still remains an option for failure of medical management in Crohn's, a retrospective cohort study from 2022 followed 14 patients who had undergone ileocolic resection from 2011 to 2021 to see if they had suffered from any complications or had undergone any additional surgeries. Five patients had four major and two minor postoperative complications with no anastomotic leakage. Six patients had endoscopic recurrence and seven had clinical recurrence (50%) at a mean of 15 months postop, one of whom required a second operation. Overall, even after surgical treatment of Crohn's disease after failure of medical management, the clinical and endoscopic recurrence rates continue to be high.
There is no evidence to support the use of probiotics for the maintenance of remission. They can only be considered for treatment of functional symptoms in IBD.
An RCT with over 700 patients found that omega-3 free fatty acids are no more than placebo in preventing relapse of Crohn's disease. A Cochrane review came to a similar conclusion, based on 2 RCTs.
No mesenteric fat targeted therapies exist at the moment and current anti-inflammatory therapies do not seem to alter it.
No firm conclusions regarding the efficacy and safety of antibiotics for maintenance of remission in CD can be drawn.
The effects of cannabis and cannabis oil on Crohn's disease are uncertain.
Exercise has been shown to decrease rates of bone loss in patients with Crohn’s disease.
Physical exercise should be considered in IBD patients with functional symptoms.

A scoping review from 2023 studied children with Crohn's disease and their physical activity participation between 1980 and April 2022. The review highlighted that physical activity participation reduced IBD-related symptoms in children, although the short- and medium-term impacts of activity on immune modulation still require further study.
The effect of psychotherapy, group therapy, and relaxation has been studied on Crohn’s disease with respect to medical and psychosocial outcomes, however the results appear to be inconsistent.

Randomized control studies are currently underway to evaluate the effects of mindfulness cognitive behavioral therapy on sleep, psychosocial distress, and quality of life in patients with inflammatory bowel disease.
No firm conclusions regarding the efficacy and safety of antidepressants in IBD can be drawn.

A randomized trial of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for patients with refractory Crohn's disease who were not surgical candidates found no benefit and significant harms. A systematic review identified only a single RCT plus four observational studies, and found high rates of transplant associated mortality (6.4%) and febrile neutropenia (83%).

Fecal transplantation is a newer method of potential Crohn's treatment that involves transferring fecal bacteria and other microbes from a healthy individual into the individual with disease. A 2023 Cochrane review RCT reported data on 21 participants receiving fecal transplant for maintenance therapy. The evidence was very uncertain about the use of transplant at 24 weeks (RR 1.21, 95% CI .36-4.14, very low-certainty evidence). There was also uncertain evidence on any serious or adverse events from this therapy. Overall, no certain conclusions could be made about the effectiveness in fecal transplantation for maintenance therapy in Crohn's disease until further evidence is collected.

A 2024 systematic review concluded the gut microbiota had a significant role in the management of IBD. The goal is to increase the beneficial bacteria including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Roseburia, Bacteroides, Ruminococcaceae, Lachnospiraceae, Firmicutes, and Bacteroidetes, and decrease the detrimental bacteria including Escherichia coli, Clostrodioides difficile, Enterobacteriaceae, and Proteobacteria. Fecal microbiota transplantation is one of the methods to accomplish this.

Enteral nutrition therapy is an option for induction of remission, given for 8 weeks. However, it is inferior to corticosteroids for induction of remission of Crohn's disease, regardless of the protein or fat composition of the formula. Long-term outcomes are no different than with steroids. A systematic review identified two trials that support use of enteral nutrition to maintain remission with similar remission rates in patients treated with either infliximab, steroids, or enteral nutrition. Enteral nutrition can also be helpful to optimize nutrition in those with severe CD especially with obstructive symptoms that require surgery.
A series of 54 individual n of 1 crossover trials compared the usual diet of an adolescent with CD or ulcerative colitis to a specific carbohydrate diet, but found no evidence of benefit.

Complementary and dietary therapies for Crohn's disease have been researched. Unfortunately, there is not enough rigorous data to support the use of these therapies as an alternative to conventional anti-inflammatory and biologic therapy in patients with active IBD.

A multidisciplinary European expert panel has made recommendations regarding the duration of therapy, and when clinicians can consider stopping drugs in patients with clinical remission and normal CRP and fecal calprotectin levels.

They concluded that azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine, and methotrexate could be withdrawn after 4 years of clinical remission and normal blood tests, while anti-tumor necrosis factor (TNF) drugs could be withdrawn after 2 years of clinical remission and normal endoscopy. For patients taking both an anti-TNF drug and an immunomodulator, the anti-TNF drug could be withdrawn after 2 years of clinical remission.

A retrospective study followed 88 patients who de-escalated treatment from immunomodulators and anti-TNF drugs to evaluate the risk of relapse. During follow-up, relapse rates were 16.7% and 52.5% in the immunomodulator discontinuation group and anti-TNF discontinuation group, respectively (p<0.001). Multivariate analysis showed that anti-TNF discontinuation (HR=3.01, 95% CI=1.22-7.43) and ileal CD location (HR=2.36, 95% CI=1.02-5.47) were predictive factors for relapse while inflammatory CD phenotype was a protective factor (HR=0.32, 95% CI=0.11-.90).
There is emerging evidence that treatment to CRP and/or fecal calprotectin targets may improve clinical outcomes, however, additional studies are required.
Patients should be hospitalized if they develop high fever, frequent vomiting, GI bleeding, severe abdominal pain, or evidence of intestinal obstruction or abscess.
Complications of Crohn’s disease include fistulae, abscesses, strictures, and obstructions.

Obstructions should be assessed with imaging studies to determine if they are adhesive obstructions or fibrotic strictures. The former can be treated with NG suction and bowel rest, the latter with corticosteroids and bowel rest. They occasionally require surgery.
Colonoscopy should be performed to traverse a stricture.

Dilation of strictures can be pursued if strictures are uninflamed, not cancer, can be traversed, or if dilation is combined with medical therapy in a patient who is naive to medical therapy, has had a gap in treatment, or is undertreated.
Inflammatory masses require IV antibiotics and steroids, while abscesses require surgical or percutaneous drainage.

Perianal fistulae can be treated medically, with ciprofloxacin and metronidazole, and if symptoms persist immunomodulators or anti-TNF agents can be added. These generally improve with medical therapy but occasionally require surgery.

Studies have been published on the use of mesenchymal stem cells in perianal Crohn's disease. Although there remain no clear guidelines on dosage, injection frequency and culture conditions, their efficacy has been shown to be higher than conventionally used methods. They can effectively induce fistula closure and avoid common side effects related to surgical treatment.
A randomized trial of 212 patients with perianal fistula found better healing with allogenic expanded adipose derived stem cells than placebo (56% vs 39% remission, p = 0.021, NNT = 6).

Osteopenia and osteoporosis are common, particularly in patients taking steroids; however, there is no evidence that favors a particular screening regimen. Updated NICE guidelines do not have routine monitoring established for patients with chronic steroid use, but they do recommend considering monitoring in patients with other risk factors such as low BMI, Vitamin D deficiency, and other comorbid conditions.

In a 2024 systemic review and meta-analysis, vedolizumab demonstrated efficacy in skin-related extraintestinal manifestations (EIMs) like erythema nodosum and joint-related EIMs including arthritis, arthralgia, spondyloarthritis, and peripheral joint diseases.
Correct fluid and electrolyte imbalances.

Patients without severe pain or obstruction may be fed orally as tolerated. Patients who cannot tolerate oral feeding should receive enteral elemental feedings or parenteral nutrition after 5 to 7 days.
Manage pain with multimodal therapy prior to opioids
Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV twice daily and metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours should be used for patients with suspected perforation, abscess, or fistula.

Crohn’s disease is characterized by intermittent episodes of pain, diarrhea, and other symptoms. Medications may decrease the severity and frequency of these episodes, but generally do not prevent them entirely. C

Risk factors for progressie disease include initially extensive disease (especially with extra-intestinal features), younger age at presentation, ileal/ileocolonic involvement, and perianal or rectal involvement.

Overall mortality is thought to be slightly higher than the normal population and is greatest in the first 2 years after diagnosis. However, a 20 year follow-up of 237 patients in Norway found no increase in overall mortality (HR 1.35, 95% CI, 0.94-1.94), and no difference in GI cancers, other cancers, or cardiovascular disease.

In a 30-year cohort study from Japan, 1108 patients were followed to investigate standardized mortality ratios (SMRs) for each cause of death of Crohn's patients. Mortality was found to be increased in patients with Crohn's disease, and SMRs were higher for Crohn's specific causes including intestinal cancer, intestinal failure, perioperative complications, and amyloidosis.
Factors like young age at diagnosis, small bowel involvement. perianal or rectal disease, and small bowel involvement are all associated with a high risk of progression.
Current evidence does not support an increased risk of lymphoma in patients with IBD at the present time.
Activity of disease is monitored by clinical signs and symptoms.
Surveillance guidelines for colon cancer, osteoporosis, and vitamin/mineral deficiencies have not been determined.
An umbrella review found moderate evidence that CD was associated with an increased risk of colorectal, small bowel, bile duct, hepatic, skin, and kidney cancers.

Each major American and European society recommends that annual colorectal screening and CA 19-9 and biliary imaging for cholangiocarcinoma be started at the time of diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC-IBD).
AASLD guidelines support cholecystectomy for polyps of any size in PSC-IBD patients given the high likelihood of malignancy.
ACG's primary sclerosing cholangitis clinical practice guidelines recommend that imaging via ultrasound or magnetic resonance and CA 19-9 be performed every 6-12 months.
Owing to the lack of formal guidelines, malignancy screening must be based on individual risk factors and tailored to specific patients.

ACG guidelines (2018) recommend that for patients at higher risk for colorectal cancer (history of dysplasia, primary sclerosing cholangitis) chromendoscopy should be utilized to enhance the ability to detect neoplasia.
A Cochrane review concluded that there is only indirect evidence that routine screening decreases mortality from colon cancer.

In patients taking a TNF antagonist, fecal calprotectin was somewhat helpful at predicting endoscopic recurrence (sensitivity 90%, specificity 80%), but less accurate at predicting clinical recurrence (sensitivity 70%, specificity 65%).
Following surgery, patients with fecal calprotectin levels <100 mcg/g were unlikely to have a recurrence.

According to 2024 meta-analysis, IBD patient's display significantly higher PLT and PCT and significantly lower MPV. Monitoring the clinical manifestations of platelet abnormalities serves as a diagnostic and prognostic information. Proactive measures should be taken to prevent consequences of platelet abnormalities in individuals with IBD.
Methotrexate is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.
An observational study found no association between mode of delivery and long-term risk of perineal disease. Women receiving cesarean section tended to be older and have more complicated CD.

A systematic review concluded that women with UC or Crohn's had small increases in the risk for preterm birth (OR 1.9, 95% CI, 1.7-2.0), still birth (OR 1.6, 95% CI, 1.03-2.4), and congenital anomalies (OR 1.3, 95% CI, 1.05-1.58).

A retrospective descriptive analysis included 47 pregnant women with IBD who delivered between March 2012 and July 2018. Obstetric and neonatal complications occurred in 55.3% and 14.86% of the IBD population, respectively. These complications included preterm birth, preeclampsia, anemia, low birth weight, postpartum hemorrhage, and neonatal death.
Presentation and diagnosis in children is similar to that in adults.

Children may develop growth delay, delayed puberty, bone demineralization, and malnutrition in addition to the typical signs and symptoms of Crohn’s disease. Good control of inflammation may reduce this adverse impact on growth, but clinical trials are lacking.
One Cochrane review evaluated the various treatment modalities with respect to their effect on growth. 6-MP was not found to have adverse effects on growth compared to placebo.
Enteral feedings were studied in two lower quality trials, and increased growth relative to corticosteroid treatment was found.
Enteral nutrition can induce remission in 60-86% of children which is particularly attractive due to replacing steroid use.

A RCT of 78 children treated with adalimumab showed improved clinical remission rates (corticosteroid free periods) with proactive monitoring versus reactive monitoring of drug trough concentrations and inflammatory markers with subsequent dose adjustments every 8 weeks.
